doc.title: Geometric Deep Learning Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges

proposal.title: Geometric Deep Learning: Grids, Groups, Graphs, Geodesics, and Gauges
proposal.gist: Deep learning architectures are instances of one geometric blueprint built from symmetry, invariance, and scale separation.
proposal.question: Geometric Deep Learning — what single principle unifies deep learning architectures across grids, graphs, groups, and manifolds? (a unifying blueprint)

children.title: Title, Authors and Contents
children.gist: The paper's title, authors, affiliations, and table of contents.

children.title: Preface
children.gist: Deep learning today resembles 19th-century geometry before Felix Klein's Erlangen Programme unified it by studying invariants under symmetry groups, motivating a parallel unification for neural networks.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning — why does deep learning need an Erlangen-style unification? (a historical analogy)

children.title: Notation
children.gist: A reference table defining the mathematical symbols used throughout the text, such as domains, signals, groups, and operators.
children.question: Notation — what symbols and conventions does the text rely on? (a reference table)

children.title: 1 Introduction
children.gist: Deep learning's success rests on representation learning and gradient descent, but real tasks have low-dimensional structure that geometric priors like symmetry can exploit to beat high-dimensional learning limits.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning — why can built-in geometric priors overcome the curse of dimensionality in deep learning? (a unifying argument)

children.title: 2 Learning in High Dimensions
children.gist: Learning generic high-dimensional functions is statistically hopeless, so neural networks must rely on inductive biases like regularity and sparsity, though these alone cannot overcome the exponential sample cost.
children.question: Learning in high dimensions — why does fitting functions in many dimensions require exploiting extra structure beyond a flexible function class? (an argument from sample complexity)

children.title: Supervised learning setup
children.gist: Supervised learning estimates an unknown labeling function from samples using a parametrised function class, with performance judged by expected loss on new data drawn from the same distribution.

children.title: 2.1 Inductive Bias via Function Regularity
children.gist: Although neural networks can approximate almost any function, this universal approximation does not remove the need for an explicit or implicit complexity measure favoring simpler, more regular interpolating solutions.

children.title: 2.2 The Curse of Dimensionality
children.gist: Classical regularity assumptions like Lipschitz continuity or Sobolev smoothness still require exponentially many samples as dimension grows, and sparsity tricks in shallow networks fail for realistic, long-range-correlated functions.

children.title: 3 Geometric Priors
children.gist: Physically structured data admits two rescuing principles, symmetry and scale separation, formalised as invariance, equivariance, and deformation-stability properties a learned function should satisfy.
children.question: Geometric priors — how do symmetry and scale separation let models escape the curse of dimensionality? (a conceptual framework)

children.title: Geometric priors via symmetry and scale
children.gist: Signals on a domain form a vector space, and exploiting the domain's symmetry and multiscale structure, as CNNs do with translation and pooling, supplies the geometric priors needed to beat high dimensionality.

children.title: 3.1 Symmetries, Representations, and Invariance
children.gist: Symmetries of a domain form a group acting on signals through representations, and functions respecting this structure are either invariant, unaffected by the action, or equivariant, transforming consistently with it.

children.title: 3.2 Isomorphisms and Automorphisms
children.gist: Different levels of structure on a domain, from bare sets to metric spaces, define correspondingly smaller symmetry groups, with automorphisms mapping an object to itself and isomorphisms relating two equivalent objects.

children.title: 3.3 Deformation Stability
children.gist: Because real-world transformations are rarely exact symmetries, functions should instead be stable to small deformations of the signal or of the domain itself, generalising strict invariance into an approximate notion.

children.title: 3.4 Scale Separation
children.gist: Multiscale, spatially localised wavelet representations remain stable under small deformations where global frequency-based Fourier representations do not, motivating hierarchical, scale-separated neural architectures that process information scale by scale.

children.title: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: Combining local equivariant layers, nonlinearities, coarsening operators, and a final invariant pooling layer yields a general recipe, the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint, underlying CNNs, GNNs and related architectures.
children.sourceHeading: 3.5 The Blueprint of Geometric Deep Learning

children.title: 4 Geometric Domains: the 5 Gs
children.gist: Grids, groups, graphs, geodesics, and gauges are five domain types whose distinct symmetry structures each generate a corresponding family of equivariant neural network operations.
children.question: The 5 Gs — what symmetry structure does each geometric domain contribute to building equivariant networks? (five domain types)

children.title: The 5 Gs framework
children.gist: The text organises geometric domains into five families, grids, groups, graphs, geodesics, and gauges, chosen not by order of generality but to highlight the key symmetry concepts each one contributes.

children.title: 4.1 Graphs and Sets
children.gist: Graphs carry permutation symmetry since their nodes have no canonical order, so valid functions must be permutation invariant or equivariant, built by aggregating neighbourhood features with shared local functions.

children.title: 4.2 Grids and Euclidean spaces
children.gist: On grids the fixed node ordering yields translation symmetry instead of permutation symmetry, and every linear translation-equivariant operator is exactly a convolution, diagonalised by the discrete Fourier transform derived from shift operators.

children.title: 4.3 Groups and Homogeneous spaces
children.gist: Convolution and Fourier analysis generalise from translations to any locally compact symmetry group acting on a domain, as demonstrated for cyclic shifts on grids and rotations on the sphere.

children.title: 4.4 Geodesics and Manifolds
children.gist: Most manifolds lack global symmetry, so invariance must instead come from intrinsic, isometry-preserving quantities like geodesic distance and the Laplacian spectrum, plus tangent-space convolutions built via parallel transport and exponential maps.

children.title: 4.5 Gauges and Bundles
children.gist: A gauge is a local frame for a tangent or feature space at each point, and functions on manifolds must be equivariant to arbitrary gauge changes, since no canonical frame generally exists.

children.title: 4.6 Geometric graphs and Meshes
children.gist: Meshes are graphs with extra geometric structure, enabling intrinsic, isometry-invariant cotangent Laplacians and functional-map methods that generalise correspondence and convolution across meshes of different resolution.

children.title: 5 Geometric Deep Learning Models
children.gist: Popular architectures, CNNs, group-equivariant CNNs, GNNs, Transformers, mesh networks and gated RNNs, all instantiate the Geometric Deep Learning blueprint for their own domain and symmetry group.
children.question: Geometric Deep Learning models — how does each popular architecture realise the blueprint's building blocks for its own domain? (eight architecture families)

children.title: From blueprint to architectures
children.gist: The following sections derive convolutional, group-equivariant, graph, set, message-passing, mesh, and recurrent architectures, in roughly increasing geometric complexity, as realisations of the one shared blueprint.

children.title: 5.1 Convolutional Neural Networks
children.gist: CNNs implement local translation-equivariant linear filters followed by nonlinearity, multiscale pooling, residual connections, and normalisation, together forming the standard recipe behind modern image-processing architectures.

children.title: 5.2 Group-equivariant CNNs
children.gist: Group convolution generalises translation-equivariant filtering to discrete rotation and reflection groups, implementable efficiently as filter transformation followed by ordinary convolution, as shown for 3D medical scans, DNA, and spheres.

children.title: 5.3 Graph Neural Networks
children.gist: Nearly all GNN layers fall into three flavours, convolutional, attentional, and message-passing, which differ in how far they let neighbour interactions depend on both endpoints' features rather than fixed weights.

children.title: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference
children.gist: Treating unordered sets as graphs with no edges, a complete graph, or an inferred adjacency respectively recovers Deep Sets, Transformers' self-attention, and the open problem of latent graph inference.
children.sourceHeading: 5.4 Deep Sets, Transformers, and Latent Graph Inference

children.title: 5.5 Equivariant Message Passing Networks
children.gist: When node features include spatial coordinates, message-passing layers can be made equivariant to rotations, reflections and translations by depending only on pairwise distances, with richer tensor representations extending this further.

children.title: 5.6 Intrinsic Mesh CNNs
children.gist: Mesh convolutions built from geodesic patches face an inherent gauge ambiguity in local coordinate frames, addressed historically by isotropic filters, fixed gauges, angular pooling, or fully gauge-equivariant parallel-transported filters.

children.title: 5.7 Recurrent Neural Networks
children.gist: RNNs summarise sequential inputs step by step and exhibit a form of shift equivariance along time once boundary conditions are handled, though plain RNNs suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients.

children.title: 5.8 Long Short-Term Memory networks
children.gist: Gated RNNs like the LSTM are exactly the architecture required for invariance to time warping, learning gates that approximate the warping rate and thereby capture long-range temporal dependencies.

children.title: 6 Problems and Applications
children.gist: Geometric Deep Learning already drives major real-world systems, from drug discovery and protein design to maps, recommenders, vision, games, speech, healthcare, and physics.
children.question: Problems and applications — where has Geometric Deep Learning already produced concrete real-world impact? (a survey of domains)

children.title: Scope of applications
children.gist: Invariances pervade real-world data, so many celebrated 21st-century machine learning successes can be reinterpreted, intentionally or not, as applications of Geometric Deep Learning principles across many domains.

children.title: Chemistry, drug design and biology
children.gist: Graph neural networks accelerate drug discovery and repositioning by predicting molecular properties and interactions, exemplified by discovering the antibiotic Halicin and by MaSIF's design of cancer immunotherapy proteins from surface meshes.

children.title: Recommenders, social networks and traffic
children.gist: Graph representation learning now powers production systems at scale, including Pinterest's and Amazon's recommenders, misinformation detection on social networks, and travel-time prediction in Google Maps and Baidu Maps.

children.title: Object recognition and game playing
children.gist: Translation-equivariant convolutional networks drove the ImageNet revolution in image classification and detection, and later powered reinforcement learning agents such as AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, and Agent57 to superhuman game performance.

children.title: Text and speech synthesis
children.gist: One-dimensional grid architectures, from dilated convolutions like WaveNet to Transformers like BERT and GPT-3, now generate human-like speech and text at industrial scale across translation and language tasks.

children.title: Healthcare applications
children.gist: Medical applications span grid-based CNNs for scans, mesh networks modelling organs and brain surfaces, graph networks of functional brain connectivity, and patient-similarity networks built from demographic or health-record data.

children.title: Physics, astronomy and virtual reality
children.gist: Particle physics, neutrino astronomy, and radio astronomy exploit graph and spherical neural networks for irregular detector geometries, while mesh-based geometric deep learning underlies modern 3D body and hand pose capture for virtual reality.

children.title: 7 Historic Perspective
children.gist: Symmetry's long history, from Platonic solids through Klein's and Noether's group-theoretic physics, re-emerges in a decades-long, multi-community lineage leading to today's graph neural networks and Geometric Deep Learning.
children.question: Historic perspective — how did ideas of symmetry evolve from classical mathematics and physics into today's Geometric Deep Learning? (a historical lineage)

children.title: Symmetry through the ages
children.gist: Symmetry has shaped mathematics and art since antiquity, from Pythagorean circles and Platonic solids to Kepler's explanation of snowflake symmetry through hexagonal particle packing.

children.title: Symmetry in Mathematics and Physics
children.gist: Group theory, developed by Galois, Lie, Klein and Cartan, became physics' language for symmetry once Noether showed every continuous symmetry implies a conservation law, later unifying forces via gauge invariance.

children.title: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning
children.gist: Early pattern-recognition work on equivariant detectors and the proven limits of perceptrons motivated multilayer networks, culminating in Fukushima's shift-invariant Neocognitron and LeCun's convolutional networks inspired by the visual cortex.
children.sourceHeading: Early Use of Symmetry in Machine Learning

children.title: Graph neural network origins
children.gist: Graph neural networks emerged independently from 1990s recursive neural architectures, 2000s fixed-point GNNs, computational chemistry's molecular graph models, random-walk node embeddings, and probabilistic graphical model message passing.

children.title: Expressive power: WL test and beyond
children.gist: GNN expressiveness is fundamentally capped by the Weisfeiler-Lehman graph isomorphism test, motivating injective aggregators like GIN and higher-order or structurally-augmented architectures aiming to exceed this representational limit.

children.title: Signal Processing and Harmonic analysis
children.gist: Harmonic-analysis ideas like scattering transforms and steerable wavelets explained early CNNs, while graph and mesh signal processing communities independently developed spectral Laplacian-based methods that later became spectral graph neural networks.

children.title: Algorithmic reasoning
children.gist: A newer strand of Geometric Deep Learning designs networks whose computations mimic algorithms' control flow and invariants, aligning GNNs with dynamic programming to emulate and extrapolate combinatorial procedures.

children.title: Naming of Geometric Deep Learning
children.gist: The term 'Geometric Deep Learning' was coined in 2015 and popularised in 2017, with the '4G'/'5G' acronym later added to name the grids-graphs-groups-gauges-geodesics framework used here.
